strengths: The paper provides a rigorous theoretical foundation: MAD is formally defined via first-passage times, shown equivalent to graph shortest-path, and proven to be the unique solution of the proposed constrained optimization problem (Theorem 1, Appendix A).

A novel, computationally cheap ReLU-based quasimetric (d_simple) is introduced with proven triangle-inequality and positive-homogeneity properties (Appendix B), and empirically shown in ablations to outperform more elaborate quasimetrics (IQE, Wide Norm).

The benchmark suite is a genuine contribution: a diverse set of environments (discrete/continuous, deterministic/stochastic, symmetric/asymmetric, noisy observations) with known ground-truth MAD enables precise, controlled evaluation that prior work in this space lacked.

Experiments are extensive and well-organized, including three complementary metrics (Spearman, Pearson, Ratio CV), ablations over latent dimension, quasimetric choice, and dataset size, plus a downstream goal-reaching planning evaluation across OGBench PointMaze/AntMaze tasks.
Reproducibility is strong: detailed hyperparameter tables and implementation descriptions are provided for all methods (MadDist, TDMadDist, QRL, Hilbert baselines).

The paper clearly situates the contribution relative to closely related work (QRL, Hilbert representations, Laplacian methods, successor features), articulating precise conceptual distinctions (symmetric vs. asymmetric, MAD vs. SSP vs. discounted temporal distance).
weaknesses: The narrative that the paper's TD-based innovation (TDMadDist) is a core contribution is undercut by the results: TDMadDist frequently underperforms both MadDist and the QRL baseline in accuracy (Figure 3) and is inconsistent in the planning task (Table 1), and the paper's explanation for this ('more effective and stable signal ... than Hilbert') does not address why it lags behind its own simpler counterpart MadDist and often behind QRL.

MadDist, the strongest-performing method, is essentially a direct regression to the trajectory index gap j-i (an upper bound on MAD) combined with a quasimetric and scale-invariant loss; this is conceptually close to Steccanella and Jonsson (2022), and the marginal technical novelty (quasimetric substitution + rescaling) is comparatively modest relative to the empirical gains claimed.

The reliance on j-i as a supervisory upper bound is only as tight as the behavior policy is efficient; for highly suboptimal or exploratory data with long trajectories, this bound can be very loose, potentially degrading the learned metric for distant state pairs. While a dataset-size ablation is included, no ablation directly varies policy optimality/trajectory efficiency to probe this limitation.

The claimed applicability to reward shaping and general goal-conditioned RL is asserted in the introduction/abstract but never empirically tested; the paper only evaluates representation quality metrics and a simple random-shooting planner, not actual downstream RL training with the learned distances as shaping signals.

No computational efficiency comparison (wall-clock time, training FLOPs) is provided despite explicit efficiency claims for the proposed quasimetric and algorithms relative to baselines like QRL's IQE.

The planning evaluation uses a simplistic random-shooting/nearest-neighbor MPC baked with access to the true simulator, which is a reasonable ablation of the metric alone but does not demonstrate whether the learned MAD embeddings would translate to gains in a realistic RL pipeline (e.g., as a reward-shaping term or in a learned policy).

strengths: The paper tackles a well-motivated problem (reward-free, action-free learning of a directed, geometrically interpretable distance) and clearly articulates the limitation of prior symmetric MAD approximations.

A systematic benchmark suite with known ground-truth MAD across discrete/continuous, deterministic/stochastic, symmetric/asymmetric, and noisy-observation settings is a useful methodological contribution that could benefit future work in this area, independent of the proposed algorithms.

The derivation connecting the LP formulation of MAD to a quasimetric-embedding relaxation (Appendix C) is clean and the uniqueness proof, while standard shortest-path reasoning, is correctly presented.
Reasonably thorough ablations (latent dimension, quasimetric choice, dataset size) and full hyperparameter disclosure in the appendix aid reproducibility.
The proposed simple ReLU-based quasimetric is computationally cheap and empirically outperforms more complex alternatives (IQE, Wide Norm) in the reported ablations.
weaknesses: The two proposed algorithms do not consistently outperform baselines: TDMadDist frequently underperforms QRL and even the Hilbert baseline is only clearly beaten by MadDist, while TDMadDist's own improvement over Hilbert is used as indirect, somewhat strained evidence of 'better parametrization' rather than a direct, convincing comparison (e.g., PointMaze Large/Giant Navigate in Table 1 where TDMadDist underperforms QRL).

The downstream planning evaluation is of questionable validity as a test of representation quality: the planner has privileged access to the true simulator for rollouts (and, in AntMaze, to dataset trajectory segments), so success partly reflects the quality of the simulator/dataset rather than purely the learned distance metric. This undercuts the claim that the embeddings are directly useful for 'goal-conditioned reinforcement learning,' since no actual policy learning or model-free control experiment is performed.

Important related baselines explicitly discussed in Section 2 are omitted from experiments — notably Steccanella and Jonsson (2022), whose formulation the paper directly builds on and critiques, and Myers et al. (2024)'s contrastive successor features. Without these comparisons, the claim of 'significantly outperforming existing state representation methods' is only partially substantiated.

Ablation studies (quasimetric choice, latent dimension, dataset size) are conducted only in the CliffWalking environment, limiting confidence that these findings generalize to the continuous, stochastic, or high-dimensional AntMaze settings that are central to the paper's claims.

Results are averaged over only 3 seeds for the main experiments (5 for ablations), and several reported standard deviations are large relative to the differences between methods (e.g., AntMaze Medium Explore 0.80±0.21 vs 0.39±0.25), making some of the comparative claims statistically fragile.
The paper offers limited theoretical insight into why the simple quasimetric outperforms IQE/Wide Norm beyond empirical observation; the explanation is largely post hoc.
No code or data release is mentioned, somewhat limiting reproducibility despite detailed hyperparameter tables.

strengths: Clear and rigorous formalization of the Minimum Action Distance (MAD) as a constrained optimization problem, including a full uniqueness proof (Appendix A) connecting it to all-pairs shortest paths on a determinized MDP graph.

Introduces a simple, computationally cheap quasimetric (dsimple) with proven triangle inequality and positive homogeneity properties, and shows empirically it outperforms more elaborate quasimetrics (IQE, Wide Norm) in ablations.

Proposes two concrete algorithms (MadDist and TDMadDist) with well-motivated loss design (scale-invariant objective, contrastive separation term, explicit upper-bound constraint, and TD bootstrapping variant), with a full derivation provided in Appendix C.

Constructs a genuinely useful and diverse benchmark suite with known ground-truth MAD spanning discrete/continuous, deterministic/stochastic, symmetric/asymmetric, and noisy-observation settings — a concrete contribution that could be reused by the community for systematic MAD evaluation.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across many environments (NoisyGridWorld, KeyDoorGridWorld, CliffWalking, PointMaze variants, OGBench PointMaze/AntMaze) against two relevant and recent baselines (QRL, Hilbert representations), using multiple complementary metrics (Spearman, Pearson, Ratio CV).
Useful ablation studies on latent dimension, quasimetric choice, and dataset size, showing robustness of the proposed approach.

Downstream goal-conditioned planning experiments (Table 1) connect representation quality to practical utility, with MadDist achieving strong success rates including in Stitch and Explore datasets that require compositional or undirected-data generalization.
Reasonably detailed implementation and hyperparameter documentation (Appendix D) supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: TDMadDist, one of the two headline algorithmic contributions, consistently underperforms MadDist and sometimes even the QRL baseline (e.g., Table 1, Figure 3); the paper's justification for its value (comparison to Hilbert alone) is somewhat post-hoc and does not strongly motivate why TD bootstrapping is a worthwhile algorithmic contribution if it underperforms the simpler MadDist in nearly all reported cases.

The MAD metric itself is a lower bound that ignores transition probabilities, which the paper acknowledges can be unrealistic in stochastic environments; the practical significance of optimizing accurately for MAD (versus SSP or other policy-dependent distances) in truly stochastic domains is not empirically demonstrated, only deferred to future work.

The planning evaluation protocol differs between PointMaze (genuine random-shooting over actions) and AntMaze (selecting trajectory segments nearest to the current state using the learned distance itself), which risks a degree of circularity — the planner's candidate generation step for AntMaze directly depends on the quality of the very distance function being evaluated, potentially advantaging methods whose embedding better clusters the offline dataset rather than purely measuring downstream task competence.

Despite extensive discussion of Laplacian-based representation methods and successor-feature-based distances in the related work, no empirical baseline from these families is included, leaving the comparison exclusively to two quasimetric/Hilbert-style methods.

Only 3 random seeds are used for the main experimental results (Table 1, Figure 3), which is relatively low for establishing statistical robustness given the reported variance in success rates and correlation metrics, though ablations do use 5 seeds.

Some baseline results (e.g., Hilbert representation scoring near 0 correlation/success in several environments) raise questions about whether the baselines were adequately tuned for the proposed benchmark suite, since these methods were originally designed/tuned for different downstream settings (e.g., on-policy or goal-conditioned RL rather than pure MAD recovery).

strengths: Provides a clean and rigorous theoretical grounding for MAD as the unique pointwise-maximal solution to a natural constrained optimization problem (Theorem 1, proved in Appendix A), which motivates the proposed learning objectives in a principled way.

Introduces two concrete offline algorithms (MadDist and TDMadDist) that natively support asymmetric quasimetric distances, addressing a genuine gap in prior work (PlanDist, Hilbert representations) that is restricted to symmetric Euclidean embeddings.

Proposes a very simple ReLU-based quasimetric (d_simple) that is shown both theoretically (Appendix B) and empirically (Appendix E) to outperform more elaborate quasimetrics (IQE, Wide Norm) while being computationally cheaper -- a nice minimalist finding.

Constructs a diverse, carefully designed benchmark suite with exactly known ground-truth MAD spanning discrete/continuous states, deterministic/stochastic dynamics, noisy observations, and strong asymmetries (key-door, cliff-walking, teleport mazes), enabling controlled comparison that is largely absent in prior quasimetric-learning literature.

Extensive ablation studies (latent dimension, quasimetric choice, dataset size, network size for baselines, constraint horizon H_c, contrastive weight w_r) support robustness claims and aid interpretability of design choices.

The downstream planning evaluation deliberately uses a weak random-shooting MPC planner with the true simulator to isolate representation quality from confounds of policy optimization, and MadDist achieves near-perfect success rates across most environments including challenging Stitch and Explore settings, providing convincing evidence that MAD accuracy translates to practical utility.
weaknesses: The 'Code Availability' statement is left blank with no actual repository link provided, which is a real reproducibility concern for a paper whose central claims rest on many implementation-specific design choices (loss weighting, quasimetric hyperparameters, network architectures) documented only in extensive appendix tables.

The benchmark suite, while diverse, was custom-designed by the authors specifically to have computable ground-truth MAD; since the proposed method's objective directly targets this quantity by construction, the evaluation may implicitly favor MAD-targeting methods over baselines (e.g., QRL, Hilbert) that optimize related but distinct notions of distance (e.g., on-policy temporal distance), raising some concern about evaluation fairness versus practical utility comparisons.

No comparison is included against Laplacian-based representation methods or Myers et al.'s time-contrastive successor features, despite both being discussed at length in Section 2 as directly relevant alternatives for defining temporal/reachability-based distances.

The strong empirical superiority of the simple d_simple quasimetric over more expressive alternatives (IQE, Wide Norm) is reported but not deeply analyzed theoretically -- it remains unclear why a simpler function class with less representational capacity for the true asymmetric distances would consistently generalize better, beyond speculative claims about optimization ease.

For stochastic MDPs, the paper acknowledges MAD is only a lower bound on the expected number of steps, yet the empirical evaluation focuses entirely on correlation/CV with this lower bound rather than validating usefulness against actual expected shortest-path/stochastic-shortest-path distances, leaving the practical implications of this approximation gap in the stochastic setting largely unexamined (deferred to future work).

TDMadDist, one of the two main proposed algorithms, is often outperformed by both MadDist and even the QRL baseline in the accuracy metrics (Figure 3, Appendix G), which somewhat undercuts the paper's framing of TD-based bootstrapping as a key contribution alongside MadDist.

strengths: The paper tackles a well-motivated problem (reward- and action-free estimation of the Minimum Action Distance) and provides a clean theoretical characterization of MAD as the unique solution to a constrained LP/shortest-path problem, with a full proof in the appendix.

The experimental suite is unusually broad for a representation-learning paper, spanning discrete/continuous state spaces, deterministic/stochastic dynamics, noisy observations, and explicitly asymmetric environments (KeyDoorGridWorld, CliffWalking, AntMaze Teleport) where ground-truth MAD is computable, enabling direct accuracy evaluation rather than only indirect downstream metrics.

Extensive ablations are provided (latent dimension, choice of quasimetric, dataset size, baseline network-size sensitivity, constraint horizon Hc, contrastive weight wr), which is good practice and helps interpret the main results.

The downstream planning evaluation is thoughtfully designed to isolate the quality of the learned distance from confounds introduced by learned dynamics models or sophisticated policy optimization, using a weak random-shooting MPC with the true simulator.

The proposed simple quasimetric (dsimple) and scale-invariant trajectory loss are reasonable, lightweight design choices that are shown empirically to outperform more complex quasimetrics (Wide Norm, IQE) at lower computational cost.
weaknesses: The core technical contributions are incremental: MadDist is essentially PlanDist (Steccanella & Jonsson, 2022) with a quasimetric substituted for a symmetric norm and a rescaled loss, and TDMadDist is a fairly direct TD/bootstrapping adaptation; the 'novel' quasimetric dsimple is a simple ReLU max/mean combination closely related to existing constructions (e.g., components of IQE). The theoretical result (Theorem 1) is a standard LP-duality/shortest-path argument.

Several reported results are suspiciously saturated (e.g., Table 1 shows MadDist achieving 1.00 ± 0.00 success in four of seven OGBench environments), which raises concern that the downstream planning benchmark may be too easy/saturated to meaningfully discriminate between methods, undermining the claimed 'decisive' superiority.

The AntMaze planning protocol deviates from pure random-shooting by selecting candidate trajectory segments from the navigate dataset using the very distance metric being evaluated to find nearest neighbors — this introduces a circularity concern that is not adequately addressed or ablated against a neutral candidate-generation scheme.

Several comparisons in the text overstate the strength of the evidence: e.g., in PointMaze Giant Navigate, TDMadDist (0.99±0.05) and MadDist (0.93±0.17) overlap substantially, yet the Discussion asserts MadDist 'outperforms...in all environments' and 'decisively outperform[s] all baselines' without acknowledging overlapping uncertainty intervals or providing significance tests.

Despite devoting substantial space in Related Work to successor-feature/time-contrastive methods (Myers et al., 2024) and Laplacian-based representation learning, no empirical comparison against either class of method is included, leaving the claimed advantages over these approaches unvalidated empirically.

The 'ground-truth' MAD for continuous environments (PointMaze, AntMaze) is itself an approximation obtained via grid discretization and Floyd–Warshall, yet is treated as exact ground truth for evaluation; this approximation could systematically favor methods (like the proposed ones) that are implicitly fit to similarly discretized/graph-like structure.

Code is not released at submission time (only a placeholder promise), limiting independent verification of the many implementation-specific choices (architecture, loss weighting, dataset curation for AntMaze Teleport) documented in the appendix.

The hyperparameter sensitivity study for wr and Hc is conducted on only two environments (AntMaze Navigate/Explore), leaving open whether the chosen defaults generalize across the full benchmark suite used for the main claims.

The constructed benchmark environments demonstrating asymmetry (CliffWalking, KeyDoorGridWorld, AntMaze Teleport) are specifically engineered to showcase directional structure; it remains unclear how much the quasimetric advantage generalizes to more naturalistic environments with milder or less obvious asymmetries.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem formulation: learning the Minimum Action Distance (MAD) purely from state trajectories, without actions or rewards, which is a practically useful setting for offline/reward-free representation learning.

Solid theoretical grounding: the paper casts MAD as the unique solution of a constrained LP-style optimization problem and proves pointwise maximality (Theorem 1), giving a principled justification for the proposed loss terms as relaxations of this program.

Two concrete, well-derived algorithms (MadDist and TDMadDist) are presented with full derivations in the appendix, and both naturally support asymmetric (quasimetric) distances, addressing a real limitation of prior symmetric approaches (PlanDist, Hilbert/Park et al. 2024b).

A genuinely useful methodological contribution is the construction of a diverse benchmark suite (NoisyGridWorld, KeyDoorGridWorld, CliffWalking, PointMaze/AntMaze variants, teleportation maze) with known ground-truth MAD, enabling precise, rather than proxy, evaluation of distance-learning methods — something prior work lacked.

Extensive empirical evaluation against multiple relevant baselines (QRL, PlanDist, PlanDist-Simple, Hilbert) using three complementary metrics (Spearman, Pearson, Ratio CV), plus a downstream planning evaluation isolating representation quality from policy-learning confounds via a deliberately simple MPC planner with the true simulator.

Good set of ablations (latent dimension, quasimetric choice, dataset size, network size for baselines, constraint horizon Hc, contrastive weight wr) that help interpret which design choices drive the gains.
Reasonably detailed implementation/hyperparameter documentation (Appendix D) supporting reproducibility, aside from the missing code link.
weaknesses: The source code link is left as a placeholder ('will be publicly released at:') with no repository provided, which undermines reproducibility at review time despite otherwise thorough hyperparameter documentation.

Several hyperparameter/design ablations (latent dimension, choice of quasimetric, dataset size) are conducted only in the CliffWalking environment; it is unclear whether conclusions (e.g., that the simple quasimetric outperforms IQE/Wide Norm) generalize across the more complex OGBench environments used in the main results.

The core algorithmic novelty is somewhat incremental: the proposed losses largely combine existing ideas (Steccanella & Jonsson's trajectory-distance objective, Wang & Isola's quasimetrics, TD-style bootstrapping), with the main new element being a simple ReLU-based quasimetric and a scale-invariant/contrastive loss combination; Theorem 1's proof is a standard shortest-path argument.

METRA (Park et al., 2024a), explicitly discussed in related work as directly relevant, is not included as an empirical baseline, leaving a gap in the comparison against state-of-the-art representation-learning methods for temporal/MAD-like distances.

Some reported results show large variance (e.g., AntMaze Medium Explore success rate 0.80 ± 0.21) without statistical significance testing, making it harder to assess how robust the claimed superiority of MadDist is in harder, less structured settings.

The OGBench AntMaze Teleport environment is described in detail in the appendix as a specific test of asymmetry, but it is not clearly reflected with corresponding results in the main tables/figures, leaving its contribution to the empirical narrative unclear.

The planning evaluation, while a useful controlled diagnostic, uses a simplistic random-shooting planner with access to the true simulator, which may not fully predict how the learned distances would perform when embedded in realistic RL/planning pipelines with learned dynamics models.
